title: Precision mode handoff: kernel signature and KV alignment
content:
Status: draft

Quick summary
- Purpose: define a compact, verifiable contract for transitions between precision modes (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ) inside the serving runtime so kernels, scheduler, and KV cache remain coherent.
- Scope: kernel capability signatures, KV-cache alignment rules when switching bitwidth/codec, scheduling heuristics for mixed-precision batches, and a lightweight verification checklist for runtime asserts.
- Audience: serving-runtime engineers, kernel authors, SREs working on rollout policies, and performance debugging.

Background / motivation
- We have many kernel implementations with different quant codecs and different assumptions about weight layout, residual dequantization, and KV cache representation. When we route requests to a model variant with a different codec, the runtime must guarantee no silent corruption of KV state or catastrophic latency regressions.
- Previous incidents: INF-2345 (silent mismatch when falling back from INT8->GPTQ during canary), performance cliffs when scheduler mixed tiny- and large-requests against different precision pools. Need a compact contract to prevent these.

Terminology (working)
- precision-mode: one of {FP32, FP16, FP8, INT8, GPTQ, AWQ} as seen by the serving runtime.
- kernel-signature: an immutable vector describing kernel capabilities (see below).
- KVC-format: on-disk / in-memory representation of KV cache (shape, dtype, packed-format marker).
- mode-handoff: an event where a request's execution path moves from a kernel or runtime component labeled with mode A to mode B.
- sticky-mode: per-session tag that indicates the preferred precision for that session (used to avoid frequent oscillation).

Kernel capability vector (KCV) - canonical fields (compact string form):
- codec: short id (e.g., "i8-gptq-v1", "awq-q4_0", "fp8-e5m2")
- supports-dequantize-on-read: boolean
- kv-store-dtype: e.g., "fp16", "fp32", "packed-i8-gptq"
- headwise-scale-support: boolean (whether kernel applies per-head scale/zero offsets)
- padding-alignment: byte alignment requirement for packed weights (8 / 16 / 64)
- evict-granularity: cache eviction granularity (tokens / seq-block)

Example KCV string (single-line):
- "codec=i8-gptq-v1;deq=true;kvdtype=packed-i8-gptq;headscale=true;align=16;evict=seq-block"

Principles for safe handoff
1) KCV compatibility first: a mode-handoff is permitted only when the downstream KCV is compatible or a validated transform exists. Compatibility rule is conservative: kvdtypes must be equal OR runtime must have a verified transform routine.
2) No silent in-place reinterpretation: changing kvdtypes with different packing or dtype requires an explicit transform job that is typed, traced, and accounted for in latency budgets.
3) Sticky-mode for sessions: opt-in per-customer or per-route sticky-mode to reduce oscillation (default: enabled for long-lived chat sessions > 60s).
4) Minimal synchronous transforms: prefer lazy background re-encoding of KV cache with a conservative fallback policy — synchronous transforms only for correctness-critical paths.

KV cache alignment and transform model
- Two modes for transforms:
  * eager-sync: perform transform during handoff; simpler semantics but adds head latency. Use for short-run jobs that cannot tolerate fallback divergence.
  * background-reencode (lazy): allow downstream kernel to operate using an adapter layer that dequantizes on-read and re-encodes asynchronously into target packed format. Adapter has a limit before it forces an eager-sync.
- Reencode contract: transform must be idempotent and reversible (where possible) for verification. We keep a transform-version tag on each KV slab.
- Memory accounting: pre-allocate a transform scratch buffer per worker (configurable cap). If scratch buffers exhausted, we fallback to conservative route (different kernel pool or reject with 503).

Adapter semantics (dequantize-on-read shim)
- Adapter API endpoints: read(kv_key) -> (dtype, data_slice, transform_version)
- Shim must present the same seq/token view to downstream kernel while keeping a reference to original backing slab.
- Adapter cost accounting: token-level billing should include adapter dequant CPU/GPU cycles and temporary memory used.

Scheduling heuristics for mixed-precision batches
- Goal: minimize tail latency for latency-sensitive routes while maximizing throughput for background work.
- Pools: maintain precision-specific worker pools and mixed-capable pools (workers with shim enabled).
- Batching rules (ordered by preference):
  1) Homogeneous batch: same precision-mode queued -> dispatch to matching pool.
  2) Homogeneous-by-KCV: same codec and kvdtypes -> allow slightly larger batch sizes (higher amortization).
  3) Mixed batch with compatibility adapter: only when expected extra per-request overhead < 8% of route's SLO; scheduler estimates adapter cost from recent metrics.
  4) Fallback: if mixed batch adapter queue grows beyond threshold, split into sub-batches or offload to reserved dedicated capacity.
- Batch formation window is adaptive: shrink window when percentiles spike for latency SLOs.

Runtime invariants and asserts (to include in debug builds)
- At handoff: assert downstream.KCV.codec in allowed_compatibility_map[upstream.KCV.codec] OR transform_available(upstream.KCV,kvdtype->downstream.kvdtype).
- At KV-read: assert slab.transform_version == session.prefers_version OR adapter_in_use == true.
- Memory invariant: allocated_scratch_buffers <= configured_cap. Trigger circuit-breaker if violated.

Metrics to emit
- handoff_attempts_total (labels: from_codec, to_codec, route, outcome)
- handoff_latency_ms_p50/p90/p99
- kv_transform_bytes_total
- adapter_read_hits / adapter_read_misses
- sticky_mode_sessions_active

Operational playbook (short)
- Canary rollout: start with background-reencode adapter only; collect adapter_read_hits and tail latency; if adapter_read_miss ratio high -> schedule a controlled eager reencode job over off-peak hours.
- Incident triage checklist:
  1) check handoff_attempts outcomes for surge of "incompatible" errors
  2) inspect adapter queue backlog per-worker
  3) validate transform_version skew across workers
  4) if memory circuit-break triggered, reduce transform concurrency or increase scratch buffer after capacity review

Developer checklist before marking kernel "production-ready"
- [ ] Provide KCV string and unit tests for compatibility matrix.
- [ ] Provide transform routine (if applicable) with correctness tests and performance budget.
- [ ] Include adapter integration test (read, concurrent reencode).
- [ ] Linear/GitHub PR must link to a Confluence entry describing packing layout.
- [ ] Add runtime asserts (debug) and metrics instrumentation.

Open questions / TODOs
- How to express partial compatibility where a kernel can read but not write a KV packing (read-only adapter)? Proposed field: "writeable=true|false" in KCV — need to discuss.
- Policy for multi-tenant KV slabs: can we reencode per-tenant or only full-slab? Concurrency implications.
- Quantized key-value compression: could we store an intermediate compressed representation to speed transforms? Prototype idea in GHPR#4721.
- UX: should customers be able to opt-out of sticky-mode per-session via request header? (security and cost implications).

Notes / scribbles
- Observed that AWQ adapters are heavier on GPU decode but light on memory; GPTQ transforms are CPU-heavy but produce denser packed slabs. Weighted placement heuristics required.
- If we standardize on a minimal on-wire KCV header for every request, downstream infra (observability, routing) can make faster decisions.

References and links
- Confluence: precision handoff spec (linked)
- GHPR#4721: prototype adapter for i8->awq conversion
- JIRA-INF-2345: incident from last quarter

Action items
- Asha: sketch adapter API + protobuf header draft by 2025-11-19.
- Marcus: microbench transform speed for i8->awq on A100; add numbers to GHPR#4721 (due 2025-11-25).
- Sofia: propose sticky-mode opt semantics and security review (due 2025-12-01).

End of doc (working draft)
